prompt: Match each part of a tracker to the question it answers.

pairs.right: How does everybody refer to this defect?
What can the team search for and count?
Which moves between states are allowed?

prompt: A team installs a tracker and starts using its default workflow. What has it skipped, by this lesson?

choices.text: Nothing: the default is the industry standard lifecycle
choices.why: There is no single standard; the default was written by somebody who never saw this product.

choices.text: Deciding its own lifecycle, which the tracker is only there to enforce
choices.why: Right: the tool is where the decision is written, not where it is made.

choices.text: Buying the add-ons that make the workflow work
choices.why: A workflow works without add-ons; the missing piece is a decision.

choices.text: Training developers on the tracker's buttons
choices.why: Buttons are the part this lesson says not to learn first.

prompt: A team writes each defect's severity in the description's text. What can it not do?

choices.text: Attach screenshots to the defect
choices.why: Attachments do not depend on where severity is written.

choices.text: Move the defect through its workflow
choices.why: States are a field of their own; severity in prose does not block them.

choices.text: List every open critical defect with a search
choices.why: Right: a value that lives only in prose cannot be searched or counted reliably.

choices.text: Assign the defect to a developer
choices.why: Assignment is its own field, unaffected.

prompt: A tester files the traceback defect with the issue type "task". What goes wrong that nobody sees?
hint: Which searches look for which type?

choices.text: The tracker refuses to save it
choices.why: Trackers accept any type; that is why the mistake is silent.

choices.text: Its id changes when somebody corrects the type later
choices.why: The id stays; the harm is in what the searches miss meanwhile.

choices.text: The developer cannot be assigned to a task
choices.why: Tasks are assigned like anything else.

choices.text: It drops out of every defect search, so lesson 16's counts are wrong
choices.why: Right: the open defects, their ages and the reopen rate all miss it.

prompt: In a Jira project whose short name is BOX, what does an issue key look like?

choices.text: BOX-42
choices.why: Right: the project's short name and a number, typed everywhere and turned into a link.

choices.text: bug/42
choices.why: That is a path; Jira keys start with the project, not the type.

choices.text: #42 in the BOX board
choices.why: Boards draw issues; the key belongs to the project and does not depend on a board.

choices.text: A long random code like 5he7q8tg
choices.why: Jira keys are meant to be read and typed by people.

prompt: A team uses Jira as it comes and never adds a severity field. What does the lesson expect?
hint: Which field is there from the start?

choices.text: Jira computes severity from the priority
choices.why: Nothing computes one from the other; they answer different questions.

choices.text: Severity gets written into the priority field
choices.why: Right: the one confusion lesson 15 spent a section untangling.

choices.text: Nothing changes: environment does the same job
choices.why: Environment says what was tested on, not how much harm the defect does.

choices.text: Jira refuses to create bugs until a severity field is added
choices.why: Jira creates bugs without one; that is exactly why the gap goes unnoticed.

prompt: Match each Atlassian product to where a tester meets it.
hint: A wiki, code, a help desk, a board.

pairs.right: The page holding the test plan and the requirements
A customer's request that turns out to be a defect
A board of cards dragged between lists

right_distractors: The test cases and their runs

prompt: What does Trello give up, compared with Jira, for tracking defects?
hint: Try dragging a card from new to closed.

choices.text: Attachments, so screenshots go elsewhere
choices.why: Trello cards take attachments.

choices.text: Enforcement: any card can go to any list
choices.why: Right: the lifecycle's rules stay a habit of the team.

choices.text: Comments, so discussion happens in chat instead
choices.why: Cards carry comments.

choices.text: Labels, so severity cannot be marked at all
choices.why: Coloured labels are one of Trello's basics, and a team uses them for severity.

prompt: A tester who knows Jira joins a team on YouTrack. What does she have to learn?

choices.text: A different way of writing a report, since its fields differ
choices.why: The report of lesson 15 fits either one, field for field.

choices.text: Everything, because the two share no concepts
choices.why: Projects, typed fields, workflows, boards and saved searches are in both.

choices.text: Mostly the names it gives to things she already knows
choices.why: Right: the five parts of section 01 are all there.

choices.text: A programming language, since YouTrack is for developers
choices.why: It is made by a company known for developer tools; using it needs no programming.

prompt: Why would a game studio end up filing defects in Assembla?

choices.text: It is the only tracker that can enforce a workflow
choices.why: Jira and YouTrack can too; that is not what sets Assembla apart.

choices.text: It has a board, which game studios need
choices.why: All four have a board of some kind.

choices.text: It was built for game testing in particular
choices.why: It was built around code hosting, not a kind of testing.

choices.text: It hosts Perforce and Subversion, and its tickets sit beside them
choices.why: Right: chosen for the repositories, with the tickets coming along.

prompt: Which free-text field holds four of lesson 15's nine fields in almost any tracker?

choices.text: The summary
choices.why: The summary is the title, one line.

choices.text: The environment
choices.why: Environment holds the version and system, when the tracker has the field.

choices.text: The description
choices.why: Right: which is why a team agrees a template for it.

choices.text: The comments
choices.why: Comments are a conversation after the report, not the report.

prompt: Why does a team agree a description template, if the tracker already requires a summary?

choices.text: Trackers reject descriptions without headings
choices.why: They accept any text; that is the problem the template answers.

choices.text: The tracker checks that fields exist, not that steps can be replayed
choices.why: Right: the template puts steps, expected and actual in the same place in every report.

choices.text: A template makes reports shorter, so more get filed
choices.why: Length is not the aim; findability is.

choices.text: So the severity can be read off the description's first line
choices.why: Severity belongs in a field of its own, where searches can read it.

prompt: Order the headings of the description template in this section.
hint: The report's own sentence: I started here, did this, expected that, saw this.
trap: Expected after actual makes the reader judge a result before knowing what it should have been.

prompt: Why are price and popularity left out of this section's five questions?
hint: One changes; one is a tiebreaker.

choices.text: Price never matters to a team that is choosing a tracker
choices.why: It matters; it changes too often for a course to quote.

choices.text: Price changes too often to quote, and popularity says little about a team's own setup
choices.why: Right: the vendors' pages answer price; popularity breaks a tie and decides nothing alone.

choices.text: All four products cost the same and are equally popular
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson says so, and it would not survive a year.

choices.text: The tester has no say in either
choices.why: A tester asked to choose has a say; these two just decide less than the five.

prompt: The theatre has one developer and one tester, and one product. What does this lesson suggest for its defects?

choices.text: Jira with a custom workflow, since a tracker should enforce the lifecycle
choices.why: Enforcement pays when habits cannot hold; two people sitting together keep them.

choices.text: A board with a list per state and a label per severity
choices.why: Right: enough for everything reported so far, until the team grows.

choices.text: No tool: Ana tells Rui about each defect in person
choices.why: Nothing would carry the history, the retest or the numbers.

choices.text: Assembla, since boxoffice is one Python file in a repository
choices.why: Assembla is chosen for repositories that need it; one Python file does not.

prompt: In the JQL `project = BOX AND issuetype = Bug AND status != Closed ORDER BY priority DESC`, the words after ORDER BY decide which defects come ___.
A company wants to replace its tracker after eight years. What decides whether it can take its defect history along?
hint: The last of the five questions.

choices.text: Whether the new tracker is more popular than the old one
choices.why: Popularity says nothing about getting the data out.

choices.text: Whether the old tracker enforced its workflow
choices.why: Enforcement shaped the history; it does not decide whether it can leave.

choices.text: Whether issues, history and attachments export in a readable format
choices.why: Right: a tracker that cannot export keeps the history hostage.

choices.text: Whether the two are made by the same company
choices.why: Same vendor or not, the data has to come out in a form the next tool reads.
